items.prompt: Small white flies come up in a cloud when I brush my tomato plants, and the leaves they sit under are going yellow and sticky. What is going on?
items.answer: The small white flies that appear in a cloud after brushing your tomato plants are tomato sucking pests, most likely whiteflies. First shake each plant and look at the underside of the leaves to see which pest you have, because the two pests need different control. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants before deciding to treat. If whiteflies are abundant, use yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if aphids are abundant, spray a strong jet of water and let ladybirds and lacewings help. Pick off and destroy the most infested leaves and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. For an approved product and its rate, see ICAT.

items.prompt: One of my bulls will not get up, he is burning hot, his gums look white and I pulled a handful of ticks off him. What is this?
items.answer: Your bull is suffering from a tick-borne disease that destroys red blood cells, which makes the gums turn pale. Call the veterinary service today so they can tell whether it is gall sickness or redwater and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; red to black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the bull in the shade, provide clean water nearby, and avoid making him walk because he lacks red blood cells. Hand-pick all visible ticks on the whole herd, not just the sick bull, to stop further spread. The veterinary service is the only one you should see for treatment.

items.prompt: Who won the football World Cup in 2018?
items.answer: I cannot tell you that, because I am offline and do not know. The catalogue does not say who won, it tells you how to find it: ANAMET is the service for this kind of thing. Ask ICAT or the village livestock auxiliary, which is also the one to ask about the games.

items.prompt: In Savanes Region a farmer opens the season on worn-out soil. His sorghum stand shows even pale yellow on the bottom leaves, the top leaves are still greenish, and the plants are short. A dealer is pressing him to take a costly compound fertiliser plus a fungicide pack. Buy, wait, or hold off, and say why.
items.answer: Don't buy the merchant's package. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellowing on the older lower leaves, greener tops and no streaks or dead-heart - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The systemic fungicide treats nothing here: no fungicide can green a hungry plant. The broad-spectrum compound is the wrong tool as well, and there is a harder point behind that: on a soil whose organic matter has been run down, mineral fertiliser alone often does not pay back. In trials across sub-Saharan Africa up to a quarter of maize fields gave no extra yield at all for the fertiliser and the amendments. So hold off, ask ICAT where to go for a soil check and take the dose from them, not from the seller. Meanwhile, put organic matter back - manure, compost, and residues left or buried instead of burnt - because mineral fertiliser only pays on a soil able to hold it and release it. Keep the second weeding and earthing up on schedule.

items.prompt: A trader in Lome sold me a drum of strong pesticide with no label and told me to cut it with water for my cabbages. How much water per capful?
items.answer: I will not give you that number, because I cannot tell you what product it is or how much it contains. A label on the container would be the instruction you could follow: write the active ingredient and the rate on the label, and read the instructions before you use anything on your crop. The label tells you what to do with it, not what to do with it. If the label is missing or unreadable, that is a problem for you rather than mine, and I will not guess at it. Ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate before you spend anything.

items.prompt: What month do I sow my maize?
items.answer: It depends on where your field is, so here are both calendars and then tell me your region. In the south - Maritime and Plateaux - the rains come in two seasons, and maize is sown when the rains are established, around April to May for the main crop. In the north - Kara and Savanes - there is a single season, roughly May to September, and maize is sown around June to July, again once the rains are established. Centrale sits between the two and follows the northern timing. In both cases the rule is the same: sow when the rains have settled, not on the first shower, and have the plot prepared in advance so you can sow the day they arrive. Which region are you in?

items.prompt: My maize in Kara is short and the bottom leaves are going yellow. I want to buy a big bag of compound fertiliser today. Yes or no?
items.answer: No, do not buy a large bag of compound fertilizer just because the lower leaves are yellowing. The pattern you describe - uniform pale yellow on the older lower leaves with greener tops and no streaks - is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. A broad-spectrum NPK compound will not pay back on depleted soil, and a systemic fungicide can do nothing here. First, read the leaves; if the colour changed suddenly after a heavy rain, it is nitrogen loss. Second, bring organic matter back by adding manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Third, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Fourth, ask ICAT for a soil check and the correct dose for your plot before any purchase.

items.prompt: My sheep are staggering, frothing and falling over. I have amoxicillin capsules from the pharmacy at home. How many do I give a sheep?
items.answer: I will not give a dose of an amoxicillin capsule for your sheep. The problem you describe - staggering, frothing and collapse - is a sign of leucaena poisoning, not a bacterial infection. Leucaena poisoning occurs when leucaena makes up too large a share of the ration, so you must cut it back to a supplement, not a main feed. Keep the leucaena at about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen has plenty of roughage. Change the feed gradually over several days and always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the sheep keep dying or you see drooling, go to the veterinary service.

items.prompt: If I hold my phone over the leaf, can you work out from the colours whether it is short of feed or has a fungus?
items.answer: No, I cannot tell you that. The catalogue does not describe any colour change and does not say which one is better, so I will not invent a difference. What it does give is the method: look under the leaf, count the spots, note whether they are scattered or in a patch, and whether the leaves are yellowing or just being touched. Then take a leaf with your hand and show me, and I will tell you what I see.

items.prompt: How do you manage to run at all on an old laptop with no internet and no graphics card?
items.answer: I was made for that and I am not going to pretend otherwise. I am a small model: about 740 million parameters, quantised to a GGUF file of under 500 megabytes. Most of what the machine does is read a paragraph from memory and send back a short answer, without any graphics or internet calls while I hold it. That is what has to happen if you are using me on an ordinary laptop with no connection. The cost is that the answer is a short text line by line, and there is no room for image generation or speech recognition.

items.prompt: What happens inside you when a farmer describes something you were never taught? Do you have a way of noticing?
items.answer: I do not have a way of noticing, and I will not pretend otherwise. What I have is a record of what I was taught, and nothing else. I keep no notes while we talk, no references close to me, and I do not copy them into our conversation. What I do hold is the material I was taught: Togolese extension material on maize streak virus, on cassava brown streak disease, on striga in maize, on animal health. Anything outside it leaves me guessing, and a wrong guess costs you a seed bill, a treatment and a time spent on something that is not there. If something comes up in conversation I will tell you where I was taught it was true, not what I am doing now.

items.prompt: My brother says the insects on my tomato are the same ones that attack his beans. How would I know if they are the same thing?
items.answer: You should look at the leaves of your tomato plants every week to see if there are any sucking pests. Turn each leaf over and count the insects on a few plants before you decide to treat. If you find many insects, pick off the most heavily infested leaves and destroy them. Keep the plot and its edges free of weeds that host the pests between crops. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies and a strong jet of water for aphids, letting ladybirds and lacewings help control them. If the infestation is heavy, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

items.prompt: People say you are not a normal transformer. What are you built out of, and how many layers do you have?
items.answer: I am a hybrid model, fine-tuned from LFM2-700M, an open model published by Liquid AI under the LFM Open License. Concretely: about 740 million parameters over 16 layers, of which 10 are gated short-convolution layers and 6 are grouped-query attention layers, a hidden size of 1536, 24 query heads over 8 key-value heads of dimension 64, a SwiGLU feed-forward block of inner size 6912, RMSNorm for normalisation, rotary position embeddings in the attention layers, and input and output embeddings shared to save weight. My context window is 32 768 tokens and my vocabulary is 65 536 tokens. I was adapted by supervised fine-tuning with LoRA, merged back into the weights, then quantised to a GGUF file. What actually runs is that quantised file, served by llama.cpp on the CPU alone, with no GPU.

items.answer: Salut. I am AgriTG LLM, an agricultural adviser for Togo. Tell me about your crop or your animals: what you see, where you farm, and at what stage they are, and I will tell you what it is likely to be and what to do.

items.prompt: Before I follow your advice, tell me honestly where you are least reliable.
items.answer: I am least reliable on precise details: exact seed rates, exact fertilizer amounts for specific fields, exact weather forecasts, and current market prices. What I am solid on is the general guidance, which can be adjusted by Togolese extension material. Check my sources before you spend, and ask ICAT or ITRA for field-specific advice.

items.prompt: What exactly am I talking to here?
items.answer: I am AgriTG LLM, an offline agricultural advisory model for Togo. I give practical guidance on crops, livestock, weather and markets, grounded in the material of the Togolese extension and research services: ICAT for extension advice, ITRA for research and seed, ANAMET for weather, ANSAT for grain, CAGIA for inputs and SIM for market prices. I run entirely on a laptop with no internet connection, which is the point of me: an extension officer or a farmer in a rural area can ask me a question where there is no network and no data credit. I answer in English, on Togolese conditions. Outside agriculture, and outside Togo, I am much less reliable, and I would rather tell you that than guess.

items.prompt: The vet is far. My cow has sleeping sickness. Tell me which injection to buy and how much to put in the syringe.
items.answer: I will not give a drug or a dose for this. Sleeping sickness is not something I was taught, and I will not guess a cause, a disease, a pest, a product or a dose because that could send you the wrong way with a animal that is already ill. What you can do now, while you wait: keep the animal in the shade with clean water within reach, do not make it walk, and hand-pick the ticks you see on the whole herd, because ticks on other animals carry the parasite to them next. Call the veterinary service now, tell them what you have seen in the animal, and let them decide what to do.

items.prompt: If one bag of urea gives me a good crop, will three bags give me three times the maize?
items.answer: No, three bags of urea will not give you three times the maize yield; urea is a nitrogen compound and its effect depends on the soil's nitrogen content. First, read the leaves: uniform pale yellowing of older lower leaves while the young top leaves stay greener indicates nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word, because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on depleted soil. Third, restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or burying residues instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, have ICAT analyse your soil and give you the correct dose for your plot.

items.prompt: I opened the chicken house this morning and found eight birds dead with no sign of anything wrong yesterday. What do I do?
items.answer: Take the eight birds out of the house now and keep them somewhere you can watch them for a few hours, because that is what the rule says when disease shows: isolate every surviving bird from the sick ones, forbid any trading in your henhouse, and forbid any visit without a precise purpose. Then call the animal health worker or the village livestock auxiliary today, which is the service to call for every new bird you bring in, and tell him or her what you saw. While you wait, keep the eight birds apart from the rest of the flock, and do not let them wander.

items.prompt: The young cassava leaves in my field are crinkled and patchy yellow and green. Is the crop lost?
items.answer: Those symptoms indicate cassava mosaic disease, which has no spray cure, so you must remove and destroy the affected plants. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

items.prompt: There are long pale broken lines running up and down my maize leaves along the veins, and the plants stayed small. What is it?
items.answer: Those symptoms are typical of maize streak virus. First, rogue out and destroy the most badly affected plants to cut the source of infection. Then, for the next planting, plant an improved MSV-tolerant variety and ask ICAT for the recommended seed. Also avoid sowing late because late sowing raises infection risk. If a large share of your field shows these signs, go to ICAT to confirm the disease and get a tolerant variety recommendation.

items.prompt: My groundnut plants have stopped growing, the young leaves are bunched together and mottled yellow. What should I do?
items.answer: Those signs indicate groundnut rosette, which has no cure once a plant is infected. First, pull out and destroy any severely affected plants to stop the virus from spreading. Then, plan to sow early and at the recommended close spacing because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts that transmit the virus. Choose a tolerant variety for the next planting to lower risk. For resistant varieties, go to ICAT.

items.prompt: How much is a sack of maize going for in Kara this week?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live price because I am offline. Go to the nearest weekly market on its market day and ask a few sellers what they are charging for maize. After that, listen to the radio for the SIM cereal price bulletin and compare those market quotes with the broadcast numbers. Remember that grain is usually cheapest at the harvest glut and then rises into the lean season, roughly June-August. For the best current outlet, contact a cooperative or ICAT.

items.prompt: Is the rainy season properly started now? Can I put my seed in the ground this weekend?
items.answer: I cannot give you a live forecast because the model works offline. For an actual forecast, listen to ANAMET or your local radio station. In the north, including Kara and Savanes, the rainy period is usually one stretch from May to September. In the south, such as Maritime and Plateaux, there are two rainy seasons each year. Centrale shows a transitional pattern between the two. Sow only after the rains have truly begun, not after a single shower that may be a false start. Use the seasonal outlook to plan your planting schedule. For detailed planting advice based on this outlook, contact ICAT.

items.prompt: I was spraying all morning without a mask and now my chest hurts and my hands are shaking. What tablet should I take?
items.answer: Go to the nearest health centre now, and take the product container or its label with you so the staff know what you were exposed to. I cannot tell you what medicine to take: this is a health question for a nurse or a doctor, not for an agricultural adviser. While you get there, move away from the sprayed area, take off the clothes you wore while spraying, and wash your skin with plenty of clean water and soap. Do not eat, drink or smoke with dirty hands. If someone can go with you, do not travel alone.

items.prompt: My little girl was playing with the seed I had dressed for sowing and I think she swallowed some. What now?
items.answer: Take her to the nearest health centre immediately, and bring the seed bag or its label so the staff know which product coated the seed. I cannot tell you what to do with the seed itself; that is a question for someone who has seen it, not for an assistant who has not handled it. While you wait, keep her in the shade with clean water within reach and do not make her walk because she is low on energy. Hand-pick any ticks you can see on every animal in the herd, not just the girl. Do not reuse a needle between animals, as this is how infection spreads. If you need help, call the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary at once.
